This entry teaches Carrier comparison as part of the fundamentals of hydrogen economy, presented the Signature way: from first principles, in plain language, building toward mastery. It sits at the Advanced tier of the teaching ladder, where each idea earns its place before the next is introduced. Signature-authored and Signature-labeled throughout.
overview: In the Signature teaching of hydrogen economy, Carrier comparison is a load-bearing idea: understand it and much of the field clicks into place. Electrolysis means splitting water with electricity, the route to green hydrogen. Transport means pipelines, tube trailers, and chemical carriers like ammonia moving hydrogen. Together these ideas give the learner working intuition, not just vocabulary. The Signature presentation stresses why each principle holds, shows where it is used in real practice, and connects it forward to the Advanced material that follows.
core_concepts: Electrolysis: splitting water with electricity, the route to green hydrogen.
Transport: pipelines, tube trailers, and chemical carriers like ammonia moving hydrogen.
key_laws: Round-trip efficiency: electricity to hydrogen and back, currently 30-45 percent.
Faraday's law of electrolysis: hydrogen produced proportional to electric charge passed.
vocabulary: Offtake: a contracted buyer making a hydrogen project bankable.
PEM: proton-exchange-membrane electrolyzers and fuel cells, fast and compact.
methods: Carrier comparison: weighing compression, liquefaction, and ammonia conversion.
history: Hydrogen powered early airships and rockets; fuel cells emerged from 1960s space programs. The 2020s hydrogen strategies of Europe, the US, and Asia now bet on green hydrogen to decarbonize steel, chemicals, and heavy transport.
key_points: Electrolysis: splitting water with electricity, the route to green hydrogen.

Governing principle: Round-trip efficiency: electricity to hydrogen and back, currently 30-45 percent.
